title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Serverless
summary: Serverless is a cloud execution model where the provider dynamically allocates and bills for compute on a per-invocation basis — functions scale to zero when idle and the operator never manages a server, OS, or orchestrator.
objectives: What is a cold start and how do you mitigate it?
How is serverless billed, and when does it become more expensive than containers?
What is the difference between FaaS and other serverless managed services?
Why are serverless functions stateless, and where do you put state?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Serverless is a cloud execution model where the provider dynamically allocates and bills for compute on a per-invocation basis — functions scale to zero when idle and the operator never manages a server, OS, or orchestrator.
Serverless as a term covers two related but distinct offerings: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms like AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, and Azure Functions; and managed higher-level services like DynamoDB, Firestore, EventBridge, S3, SQS, and API Gateway whose compute is invisible to the user. The defining property of FaaS is that you upload code (a function) and the platform runs it in response to events — HTTP requests, queue messages, object uploads, timers, or stream changes — without you provisioning or paying for an idle server. AWS Lambda launched at re:Invent 2014, and within two years it had reshaped how event-driven workloads were built. The billing model is striking: you pay per request (typically $0.20 per million on Lambda) and per GB-second of execution (memory allocated × duration in 1-ms increments), with no minimum spend. A function that runs 100ms a day on 128MB costs essentially nothing; the same workload on an always-on t3.micro costs $8/month. This pricing asymmetry is the core economic argument for serverless.

The second property is scale-to-zero. When a Lambda function has not been invoked for a few minutes, the platform reclaims its execution environment. The next invocation triggers a cold start: the platform allocates a fresh micro-VM (AWS Firecracker, ~125ms boot), downloads the function code, initializes the runtime (Node, Python, Java), and runs your initialization code before the first request can be served. Cold-start latency ranges from 50ms for a minimal Node function to several seconds for a Java function with a heavy Spring context. After the first invocation, the environment is kept warm for subsequent requests, and warm invocations add only a few milliseconds of overhead. For latency-sensitive workloads this is the central trade-off: you get infinite scale and zero idle cost, but the first request after idle pays a latency tax. Provisioned concurrency — Lambda's feature for keeping N environments warm — buys back the latency at the cost of an always-on hourly charge, partially eroding the serverless economic advantage.

The third property is operational simplicity. There is no AMI to patch, no Kubernetes cluster to upgrade, no autoscaling policy to tune, no node pool to drain. The provider handles all of it. This shifts engineering effort from operations to code, and it makes serverless especially attractive for event-driven glue code: a Lambda that processes an S3 upload, transforms a DynamoDB stream record, fans out an EventBridge event, or runs a nightly cleanup cron. Netflix's media pipeline uses Lambda functions to trigger video encoding jobs when new content lands in S3 — the trigger fires within seconds of upload, scales to thousands of concurrent encoders when a new series drops, and costs nothing between releases. Coca-Cola's vending machine telemetry flows through IoT Core into Lambda functions that validate, enrich, and write to DynamoDB, replacing an always-on fleet of EC2 instances that had been 80% idle outside business hours.

The fourth property is the bounded execution model. Lambda functions run for at most 15 minutes, can use up to 10GB of memory, and have a per-account concurrency limit (default 1000) that can be raised by request. They are stateless: any in-process state is lost between invocations unless explicitly persisted to external storage. This forces a functional programming style — pure functions, immutable inputs, side effects only via external services — and pushes state into DynamoDB, S3, ElastiCache, or a database. Workloads that do not fit this shape (long-running batch jobs, persistent connections like WebSockets, GPU inference) are poor fits for FaaS, though newer offerings like AWS Fargate for containers, Lambda with longer timeouts (still capped at 15 minutes), and specialized services like SageMaker for ML address some of these gaps. Amazon Prime Day's order processing leverages Lambda for individual stateless steps in a larger Step Functions workflow, keeping each function small and stateless while the orchestrator manages state and retries.

The fifth property is the integration model. Serverless functions rarely run alone; they sit in an event-driven pipeline built from managed services. A typical web backend looks like: API Gateway (HTTP) → Lambda (business logic) → DynamoDB (state) with Cognito for auth, SQS for async decoupling, SNS for fan-out, and EventBridge for routing. This composition is powerful but introduces a new operational challenge: debugging across a dozen managed services, each with its own logging format and observability model, is harder than debugging a monolith. AWS X-Ray, Datadog, and Lumigo address this with distributed tracing that follows a request across service boundaries, but the cognitive load is real. The trade-off is velocity versus observability — you can build a feature in an afternoon that would have taken a week on EC2, but diagnosing a production issue may take longer because the request hops through services you do not control.

The economics and architecture pattern that emerges is "serverless-first." For low-volume APIs, async glue, scheduled jobs, and stream processors, FaaS is almost always the right answer on cost and velocity grounds. For high-volume steady-state APIs, the per-request cost of Lambda (around $1.50 per million requests at 256MB and 200ms) exceeds the per-request cost of an ECS or EKS service once you cross roughly 5–10 million requests per month sustained — at that scale, you migrate hot paths to containers. The mature pattern is hybrid: Lambda for the long tail of less-trafficked endpoints and for event-driven work, containers or managed Kubernetes for the high-throughput core, and managed databases for state. Real-world examples reinforce this: Netflix uses Lambda for the encoding trigger fan-out but runs the encoders themselves on EC2; Coca-Cola uses Lambda for vending telemetry but runs analytics on EMR; Amazon itself uses Lambda for thousands of internal automation tasks but runs retail on larger services. Serverless is not a replacement for other compute models — it is the best tool for a specific class of workloads, and the architect's job is to know which class.

between invocations ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------------------------------------------------------+ | Serverless Platform (AWS Lambda) | | | | Events: HTTP | S3 put | SQS | DynamoDB stream | cron | | | | | v | | +------------------+ | | | Event Router | | | +--------+---------+ | | | | | +--------------+--------------+ | | | | | | | v v v | | +----------+ +----------+ +-----------+ | | | Warm Env | | Warm Env | | Cold Env | | | | (reuse) | | (reuse) | | (booting) | | | | +3ms | | +3ms | | +300ms | | | +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +-----+-----+ | | | | | | | +------+-------+-------+-------+ | | | | | | v v | | +------------+ +-----------+ | | | DynamoDB | | S3 / SQS | | | +------------+ +-----------+ | | | | Billing: $0.20 / 1M reqs + $0.0000166667 / GB-sec | | Scale: 0 --> 1000 concurrent (default account cap) | +-----------------------------------------------------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. An event (HTTP request via API Gateway, S3 upload, SQS message, DynamoDB stream change, or timer) triggers an invocation of the function. 2. The platform routes the invocation to a warm execution environment if one exists; otherwise it provisions a new Firecracker micro-VM, loads the code, and initializes the runtime, incurring a cold start of 50ms to several seconds. 3. The function executes with the configured memory and timeout (up to 10GB, up to 15 minutes), reading and writing state only through external services since the execution environment is stateless. 4. The platform bills per request plus GB-seconds (memory × duration in 1-ms increments) and reclaims the environment after several minutes of idle time, returning the function to zero cost when traffic stops.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Lambda / Cloud Functions / Azure Functions style runtime.
- Serverless_engine.py - runnable mock of a FaaS platform.
- Models: cold/warm execution environments, per-invocation billing,
- Concurrency scaling, and a step-function pipeline.
- Find a warm env, else provision a cold one
- Run the user handler, measure duration
- Purge environments idle beyond TTL
- A simulated "init hook" representing heavy SDK/client setup

**Defines:** `Invocation`, `ExecutionEnv`, `ServerlessPlatform`

```python
# serverless_engine.py - runnable mock of a FaaS platform.
# Models: cold/warm execution environments, per-invocation billing,
# concurrency scaling, and a step-function pipeline.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Any
import time, uuid, random

@dataclass
class Invocation:
    request_id: str
    event: Dict[str, Any]
    started_at: float
    duration_ms: float = 0.0
    billed_mb_ms: int = 0
    cold_start: bool = False

@dataclass
class ExecutionEnv:
    env_id: str
    function: str
    memory_mb: int
    last_used: float
    invocations: int = 0
    state: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # user-defined warm state

    def is_warm(self, now: float, idle_ttl: float = 600.0) -> bool:
        return (now - self.last_used) < idle_ttl

class ServerlessPlatform:
    """Lambda / Cloud Functions / Azure Functions style runtime."""
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.functions: Dict[str, dict] = {}        # name -> config
        self.envs: Dict[str, List[ExecutionEnv]] = {}  # name -> warm envs
        self.history: List[Invocation] = []
        self.account_concurrency = 1000
        self.cold_start_ms = 250
        self.warm_overhead_ms = 3
        self.price_per_req = 0.0000002          # $0.20 / 1M
        self.price_per_gb_sec = 0.0000016667

    def deploy(self, name: str, handler: Callable, memory_mb: int = 256,
               timeout_s: int = 15, init_hook: Optional[Callable] = None):
        self.functions[name] = {
            "handler": handler, "memory_mb": memory_mb,
            "timeout_s": timeout_s, "init_hook": init_hook,
        }
        self.envs.setdefault(name, [])
        print(f"[deploy] {name}: {memory_mb}MB, timeout={timeout_s}s")

    def invoke(self, name: str, event: dict) -> Any:
        if name not in self.functions:
            raise RuntimeError(f"unknown function {name}")
        cfg = self.functions[name]
        now = time.time()
        # Account-wide concurrency cap
        active = sum(len([e for e in envs if e.is_warm(now)])
                     for envs in self.envs.values())
        if active >= self.account_concurrency:
            raise RuntimeError("account concurrency exhausted (throttle)")

        # Find a warm env, else provision a cold one
        cold = False
        env = None
        for e in self.envs[name]:
            if e.is_warm(now):
                env = e
                break
        if env is None:
            env = ExecutionEnv(f"env-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]}",
                               name, cfg["memory_mb"], now)
            self.envs[name].append(env)
            if cfg["init_hook"]:
                cfg["init_hook"](env)        # heavy init: SDK clients, etc.
            cold = True
            print(f"[invoke] {name}: COLD start env={env.env_id} "
                  f"(+{self.cold_start_ms}ms)")

        inv = Invocation(request_id=f"req-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
                         event=event, started_at=now, cold_start=cold)
        overhead = self.cold_start_ms if cold else self.warm_overhead_ms
        # Run the user handler, measure duration
        t0 = time.time()
        result = cfg["handler"](env, event)
        user_ms = (time.time() - t0) * 1000.0
        inv.duration_ms = overhead + user_ms
        inv.billed_mb_ms = int(cfg["memory_mb"] * (inv.duration_ms / 1000.0))
        env.last_used = time.time()
        env.invocations += 1
        self.history.append(inv)
        # Purge environments idle beyond TTL
        self.envs[name] = [e for e in self.envs[name] if e.is_warm(env.last_used)]
        return result

    def bill(self) -> dict:
        reqs = len(self.history)
        gb_sec = sum(inv.billed_mb_ms for inv in self.history) / 1024.0
        cost = reqs * self.price_per_req + gb_sec * self.price_per_gb_sec
        colds = sum(1 for inv in self.history if inv.cold_start)
        return {"requests": reqs, "gb_seconds": gb_sec,
                "cold_starts": colds, "cost_usd": round(cost, 6)}

# ---- demo ----
if __name__ == "__main__":
    plat = ServerlessPlatform("Lambda")

    # A simulated "init hook" representing heavy SDK/client setup
    def init(env):
        env.state["db_client"] = "<connected>"
        env.state["cache"] = {}

    def order_handler(env, event):
        # warm path: reuse db_client and cache
        if "item" not in env.state["cache"]:
            env.state["cache"]["item"] = f"<loaded from DB via {env.state['db_client']}>"
        return {"status": "OK", "item": event.get("item"),
                "served_by": env.env_id, "warm_invocations": env.invocations}

    plat.deploy("process-order", order_handler, memory_mb=256, init_hook=init)

    # Simulate a burst of requests with idle gaps to trigger cold starts
    print("\n-- burst 1 (likely cold) --")
    for i in range(5):
        r = plat.invoke("process-order", {"item": f"sku-{i}"})
        print(f"  resp: {r}")

    print("\n-- idle 11 min (env reaped) --")
    # Manually age the env to simulate idle TTL expiry
    for env in plat.envs["process-order"]:
        env.last_used = time.time() - 700

    print("\n-- burst 2 (cold again) --")
    for i in range(5):
        r = plat.invoke("process-order", {"item": f"sku-{i+5}"})
        print(f"  resp: {r}")

    print("\n-- bill --")
    print(plat.bill())
```

It consists of micro-VM boot (AWS Firecracker, ~125ms), runtime initialization (loading Node, Python, or JVM), and your function's init code (SDK clients, heavy imports, config fetches).

quiz.explanation: Serverless functions are stateless because the platform can spin up or tear down execution environments at any time, and a single warm environment may serve many concurrent invocations or none for hours. Any state held in process memory is unreliable — it may disappear at any moment, it is not shared between environments, and it cannot be relied on for the next invocation.
